title: From the Kitchen to the Charts
subtitle: Reportaje de una revista de música sobre The Clifton Cats

paragraphs: Two years ago, The Clifton Cats were playing to thirty people on a Friday night in a Bristol pub, most of whom had come for the cheap beer rather than the music. Today their first album, Clifton Road, is being described as one of the surprises of the year, and the band is about to leave on a twenty-date European tour. When I meet the singer, Sam Turner, in a London café, he still seems slightly shocked by it all. "Honestly, I keep waiting for someone to tap me on the shoulder and tell me there's been a mistake," he says, stirring a third sugar into his coffee.

Turner, who is thirty-two, grew up a few streets away from the house that gave the album its name. For almost ten years he combined music with a part-time job as a waiter, and he lived in a shared house on Clifton Road with a nurse and a Spanish designer. "People think being in a band is glamorous," he laughs. "Believe me, it isn't. I used to finish a gig at midnight, get home at one and be serving breakfasts at eight. My flatmates must have hated me. I'd come in late, make toast, leave the kitchen in a mess and play the guitar until two." He pauses. "Actually, they did hate me, a bit. But they also came to every single gig."

The other three Cats have equally unglamorous backgrounds. The drummer, Kemi Adeyemi, teaches maths at a secondary school and spent most of last year marking homework on the tour bus, or rather on the back seat of a borrowed van. The bass player, Tom Riley, repairs bicycles, and the keyboard player, Jess Holt, is a primary school music teacher who joined the band after answering an advert on a supermarket noticeboard. "Jess is by far the best musician in the band," Turner says. "She can read music, which makes her a genius as far as the rest of us are concerned. The rest of us learned everything from YouTube and from making mistakes in front of people." The four of them have been playing together for six years, and they insist that nothing has changed between them. "We argue about the same things we always argued about," Kemi tells me later on the phone. "Who forgot the cables, who ate the last sandwich. The only difference is that now someone else drives the van."

The band's lucky break came on a cold February night at The Old Duke, a small pub near the harbour where they had been playing every Friday for three years. A music producer from London, who is said to have been in Bristol for a wedding, walked in to get out of the rain. He stayed for the whole set. "If it hadn't been raining that night, none of this would have happened," Turner says. "I think about that a lot. We owe our whole career to the British weather."

Three months later the producer called with an offer: six months in London to write and record an album. For Turner, the decision wasn't as obvious as it might seem. "I was thirty, I had a job, a room I could afford and friends I loved. Moving to London to chase a dream at my age felt a bit ridiculous." It was his flatmates, he admits, who convinced him. "They sat me down in the kitchen and told me that if I didn't go, I'd regret it for the rest of my life. Priya also pointed out that the kitchen would be much tidier without me. She had a point."

His farewell gig at The Old Duke has already become a small local legend. Halfway through the concert, the electricity went off, and the pub was left in complete darkness. Rather than stopping, Turner picked up the old acoustic guitar he had brought with him, climbed onto a table and carried on playing. The whole pub joined in. "It was the best night of my life," he says simply. "Someone filmed it on their phone, and the video has been watched more than a million times. I wish I'd known that at the time. I'd have washed my hair."

The album itself was recorded in just six weeks, in a studio in north London that the band could only afford to rent at night. Despite the time pressure, it sounds anything but rushed. Most of the eleven songs are thought to have been written in that famously untidy kitchen in Bristol, and it shows. These are songs about ordinary things: missed buses, late shifts, rent day, an argument about the washing-up that turns into a love song. Critics have praised the album for its warmth and humour, while one newspaper described Turner as "the most honest songwriter Bristol has produced in years".

Those six weeks in London were not easy. The band shared a tiny two-bedroom flat above a launderette, and Turner, as the only one who could cook, found himself making pasta for four at three in the morning. "We'd finish recording at sunrise, sleep until the afternoon, and start again in the evening," he remembers. "I don't think I saw daylight for a month." He missed Bristol badly. "London is amazing, but it's enormous. In Bristol, you walk into a pub and someone knows your name. In London, you walk into a pub and someone charges you nine pounds for a pint." To cope with the homesickness, he would ring Clifton Road almost every night, and his flatmates would hold the phone up while they cooked so that he could hear the kitchen. "Some people meditate," he says. "I listened to my friends arguing about the washing-up."

Not all the reviews have been positive, however. One well-known music website accused the band of being "too nice" and claimed that some of the songs sounded "like they were written for a television advert". Turner shrugs when I mention it. "I read it, obviously. You always read the bad ones. Annoyingly, they had a point about one song, which I'm not going to name. We should have left it off the album, but we'd run out of time." He smiles. "My mum, on the other hand, thinks it's the best album ever made, so it balances out."

Success has brought its own problems. The band has had to get used to being recognised in the street, and Turner admits that the last few months have been exhausting. "We'd been working sixteen-hour days for weeks before the album came out, and then suddenly there were interviews, photo shoots, radio sessions. I had my hair cut by a professional for the first time in my life. Before that, Priya used to do it in the kitchen with the scissors we used for opening packets." He seems genuinely puzzled by some of the attention. "Someone asked me last week what my 'creative process' was. I told them it was mainly tea and panic."

What hasn't changed, apparently, is his loyalty to the people who helped him. When the band was offered a deal by a much bigger record company last month, Turner reportedly insisted on keeping the producer who had first heard them in that rainy Bristol pub. "He took a risk on us when nobody else would," he says. "You don't forget that. Well, you'd better not, anyway. My mum would kill me." He still phones his old flatmates every Sunday, and he has promised to save them seats at the band's concert in Madrid in June. "Lucía's brother is flying in from Dublin, and Lucía has told me that if we don't play the song about the washing-up, she'll never speak to me again. So that's the set list sorted."

The tour begins in Amsterdam next month and will take in Berlin, Paris, Lisbon and Madrid before ending, fittingly, with two nights at a large concert hall in Bristol. Tickets for both Bristol nights sold out in under an hour. Turner admits he finds this slightly terrifying. "Two years ago we were playing to thirty people, half of whom were watching the football on the pub television. Now three thousand people are going to be standing in front of us, singing along. I keep wondering whether we're going to be good enough."

So what advice would he give to a young musician playing to an empty pub on a wet Friday night? He thinks for a long time before answering. "Keep going. Play every gig as if it's the most important one, because one day it will be, and you won't know until afterwards. Be nice to the bar staff, they're the ones who'll tell you if you're any good. And always, always carry a spare acoustic guitar. You never know when the lights are going to go out."

As we leave the café, a teenager at the next table asks shyly for a photo. Turner looks almost embarrassed, but he agrees, and then insists on paying for her hot chocolate as well as our coffees. "Old habits," he says, winking. "I was a waiter for ten years. I can't watch someone drink something without wanting to bring them a biscuit."
Clifton Road is out now. The Clifton Cats' European tour starts on 2 May.

glossary.tap me on the shoulder: darme un toquecito en el hombro
glossary.fittingly: como no podía ser de otra manera

questions.question: How does Sam feel about the band's success, according to the first paragraph?
options: He still finds it hard to believe.
He thinks they deserved it much earlier.
He is tired of talking about it.

questions.question: What does Sam suggest about his time living on Clifton Road?
options: He never had time to see his flatmates.
He was a difficult flatmate, but his friends supported him.
His flatmates didn't like his music.

questions.question: Why does Sam say the band "owe" their career to the British weather?
options: Their best song is about the rain.
Rain stopped the producer from going to another concert.
The producer only came into the pub to escape the rain.

questions.question: Why did Sam hesitate before accepting the producer's offer?
options: He felt too old to move to London for a dream.
He didn't trust the producer.
His flatmates asked him to stay.

questions.question: What does Sam say about the negative review?
options: He refused to read it.
He partly agrees with it.
He thinks the website was paid to write it.

questions.question: In paragraph 8, "tea and panic" is…
options: the name of one of the band's songs.
a criticism of journalists.
a humorous way of saying he has no special method.

questions.question: What does Sam's decision about the producer show?
options: He is loyal to the people who helped him at the start.
He prefers working with small companies.
His mother makes his business decisions.

questions.question: What is the writer's attitude towards Sam in the final paragraph?
options: Critical: he suggests Sam is pretending to be modest.
Warm: he shows that Sam is still kind and unpretentious.
Neutral: he only reports what Sam says.

exam_practice.title: Uso del inglés · Una palabra por hueco
exam_practice.instructions: Como en los exámenes oficiales: escribe una sola palabra en cada hueco.

items.text: The album ___ described as one of the surprises of the year. The producer is said to ___ been in Bristol for a wedding. ___ the time pressure, the album doesn't sound rushed.
items.hint: Is said to have + participio, para algo pasado. Despite + nombre.

items.text: The band ___ been playing at The Old Duke for three years when the producer walked in. If it ___ been raining, he wouldn't have gone in.
items.hint: Acción que duraba hasta un momento del pasado: had been + -ing.

items.text: One website accused the band ___ being "too nice". The critics praised the album for ___ warmth. Sam had his hair cut ___ a professional for the first time.
items.hint: Accuse someone of + -ing. Praise something for…

exam_practice.title: Formación de palabras
exam_practice.instructions: Escribe una palabra derivada de la que está entre paréntesis (por ejemplo, DECIDE → decision).

items.text: Being in a band isn't as ___ (GLAMOUR) as people think. ___ (ANNOY), the bad review had a point. Sam seems ___ (GENUINE) puzzled by the attention.
items.hint: Adjetivo con -ous; adverbios con -ly que comentan toda la frase.

items.text: The band has shown great ___ (LOYAL) to their producer. The tickets sold out, which Sam finds ___ (TERRIFY). ___ (APPARENT), he still phones his old flatmates every week.
items.hint: Nombre abstracto: -ty. Adjetivo que describe la cosa: -ing.

exam_practice.title: Transformaciones
exam_practice.instructions: Completa la segunda frase para que signifique lo mismo que la primera. Usa la palabra entre paréntesis sin cambiarla y entre dos y cinco palabras.

items.text: "I regret not leaving that song off the album." → We ___ (SHOULD) that song off the album.
items.explanation: Should have + participio expresa que algo habría sido lo correcto y no se hizo.

items.text: "It's a pity I didn't know about the video at the time." → I ___ (WISH) about the video at the time.
items.hint: Wish + past perfect para lamentar algo del pasado.

items.text: "A professional cut my hair for the first time." → I ___ (HAD) by a professional for the first time.
"People believe that Sam wrote most of the songs in his kitchen." → Sam ___ (THOUGHT) most of the songs in his kitchen.
items.explanation: Pasiva impersonal: sujeto + is thought to have + participio para hechos pasados.

items.text: "You should not forget the people who helped you." → You ___ (BETTER) the people who helped you.
items.hint: Had better not + verbo, sin to.

items.text: "Most of the songs were written by Sam, but the producer chose the order." → Although ___ (WROTE) most of the songs, the producer chose the order.

a sudden chance that leads to success
done too quickly, without enough care
to move your shoulders up to show you don't know or don't care
confused because you don't understand something
staying faithful to a person or group
in a way that is right for the situation
to close one eye quickly as a friendly signal
